headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 3 studies yielded an effect size of 0.75 (95% CI: 0.4–1.4), indicating no statistically significant association between Vitamin B6 and renal cell carcinoma. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 87.30%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.

effect_size.excerpt: The ORs for the upper quintile of intake when compared with the lowest one were 0.80 (95% confidence interval, CI = 0.59-1.08) for retinol, 0.82 (95% CI = 0.61-1.10) for alpha-carotene, 0.90 (95% CI = 0.68-1.20) for beta-carotene, 0.94 (95% CI = 0.73-1.21) for beta-criptoxanthin, 0.85 (95% CI = 0.63-1.14) for lutein/zeaxanthin, 0.76 (95% CI = 0.57-1.01) for vitamin D, 0.75 (95% CI = 0.55-1.01) for thiamine, 0.88 (95% CI = 0.66-1.19) for riboflavin, 0.85 for vitamin B6 (95% CI = 0.64-1.13), 0.85 (95% CI = 0.64-1.12) for folate and 0.80 (95% CI = 0.60-1.07) for niacin. No meaningful associations emerged for lycopene (OR = 1.11).
